sections.h2: How can a Largo homeowner sell quickly?
sections.html:
The options are a cash sale, an agent listing and a sale you handle yourself. A cash buyer shortens the timeline because there is no loan approval and no appraisal gap to worry about.

Listing may bring more money from a financed buyer, though showings, inspection requests and a lender's schedule stretch the process. A house with an aging roof, code problems or an estate attached often moves better to a direct buyer. A well kept house with time on the clock deserves a listing opinion alongside any cash offer.

  • Compare offers by closing date and net proceeds.
  • Ask who covers title charges and deed tax.
  • Verify that no lien or tax balance will block the deed.

sections.h2: Why is the city called Largo?
sections.html:
Residents picked the name in 1886 while the Orange Belt Railroad was coming through, because a station needed a named stop. Some wanted Luluville, after the daughter of a prominent resident, but they chose Largo for the town's large lake, which the Cross Bayou Drainage District later drained completely.

The city says its central location and farmland made it the center of the area's citrus industry, which earned it the title Citrus City. Largo was incorporated in 1905, and in 1913 became the first town in Florida, and the second in the nation, to adopt a town manager form of government. A hard freeze late in the 1920s followed by the Depression forced the city back to its original 1905 boundaries as a town.

Population grew from about 1,500 in 1950 to over 5,300 a decade later. After a freeze in 1962, grove owners sold off land and builders put up homes, and by 1970 more than 22,000 people lived here. Today the city says it has over 80,000 residents and a base of medical, technology, manufacturing and hospitality employers. Before the freeze, groves surrounded the town, and Dansville was built to house the workers who picked and packed the fruit.

sections.h2: What neighborhoods and heritage sites shape Largo's housing?
sections.html:
Housing in Largo mostly reflects the postwar and post-freeze building years, with older pockets that trace back to the citrus era.

The city highlights Dansville, which grew from a 1946 purchase of 80 acres by Dan Henry in southwest Largo. He built a home for his family, invited other African American families to settle and provided housing for citrus workers. The city's history page also lists Heritage Village and the Largo Historical Society among local keepers of the archive.

The city names several local archives: the Largo Public Library, the Pinellas County African American History Museum and the Pinellas County Historic Preservation Board among them. If your house is old enough that its past could add interest, those are places to look for photographs or permit history.

For a seller, the takeaway is to know your build year and keep records of upgrades. A buyer's inspector will ask for the roof date and the age of the air conditioner and the electrical panel.

sections.h2: How does the Pinellas tax collector handle a Largo bill?
sections.html:
Bills go out on the last business day of October, payments are accepted from November 1, and April 1 starts delinquency.

The Pinellas County Property Appraiser sets values, and the tax collector mails and collects the bills. Up to two owners print on a bill, and address changes go through the appraiser, not the collector. If your mortgage company escrows your taxes, the notice you receive may be informational only. For the 2026 bills the collector lists the tax certificate sale as May 28, 2027.

Besides paying in full, the collector offers an installment plan for estimated bills over $100, with applications from November 1 through April 30. A partial payment plan takes payments of $100 or more but forfeits early discounts, and homestead owners may apply to defer taxes by March 31, which creates a lien and accrues interest.

sections.h2: What happens if a Largo property tax bill is not paid?
sections.html:
The sequence ends in a possible tax deed auction, and each step has a published deadline.

After April 1 interest and costs are added, and Florida law prohibits partial payments of delinquent real estate taxes. By June 1 the collector sells a tax certificate on the parcel, awarded to the bidder who accepts the lowest interest, with unsold certificates struck off to the county at 18 percent. After two years the holder can start a tax deed application, and the collector mails a warning letter each February to owners at risk, with a deadline of the last business day of March.

Once a deed action begins, all outstanding taxes roll into a single amount plus interest and costs, and only full payment stops it. Personal checks are not accepted for tax deed payments, only cash, wire or certified funds.

sections.h2: What else should a Largo seller know about taxes and deeds?
sections.html:
The deed carries Florida's 70 cents per $100 documentary stamp tax, collected by the clerk at recording.

The revenue department lists quitclaim deeds, deeds in lieu of foreclosure and contracts for deed among taxable documents, so a family transfer for value is not automatically exempt. A mortgage on the property counts as consideration. Recording is $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 for each additional page, and two witnesses must see the deed signed.

If you have rented the house to short-term guests, the Pinellas tax collector's FAQ describes a 6 percent tourist development tax on stays of six months or less, with a 7 percent state sales tax on top for a total of 13 percent. Returns are due even when no rent was collected, and a late return carries a $50 minimum penalty. Settle those accounts before you close.

  • Close or update your tourist tax account if you rent short term.
  • Collect lease copies for long-term tenants.
  • Ask the title company what it needs for the deed.

sections.h2: What about tenants or an inherited Largo house?
sections.html:
Tenants and estates both add timelines. Rental houses carry one more item: Pinellas taxes furniture and equipment in rental properties as tangible personal property, billed to whoever owns it on January 1, and any unpaid lien on it survives a sale of the property. Check that those accounts are paid.

A year-to-year tenancy ends on 60 days' notice, a quarter-to-quarter one on 30 and a week-to-week one on 7. A sheriff posts 24 hours' notice before returning possession after a court judgment. For an estate, Florida has had no state estate tax for people who died after 2004, and the personal representative no longer files the state forms.

faqs.a: Pinellas County. The Pinellas County Property Appraiser sets values and the Pinellas County Tax Collector mails the bills.

faqs.q: When do Pinellas tax bills go out?
faqs.a: On the last business day of October, and payment is accepted from November 1. April 1 is the delinquency date.

faqs.q: Can I pay a Largo tax bill by credit card?
faqs.a: Yes, online, with a 2.50 percent convenience fee from the payment processor. eChecks are free. Delinquent taxes cannot be paid by personal check.

faqs.q: What stops a tax deed process?
faqs.a: Full payment of the rolled-up amount, with interest and costs, in cash, wire or certified funds. Installments do not stop it once the action has started.

faqs.q: What is Largo's tourist tax if I rented the house?
faqs.a: The Pinellas tax collector describes 6 percent tourist development tax on rentals of six months or less, plus 7 percent sales tax. Ask that office to close the account when you sell.
